blocks.prompt: The Otter With a Pocket
blocks.text: A whale stays warm in the cold sea with a thick layer of fat. A sea otter has no fat like that. It has fur instead, and its fur is the thickest fur of any animal on Earth. Tiny bubbles of air hide down in that fur and keep the cold water off its skin. The otter has a pocket too. It is a fold of loose skin under its arm. The otter keeps its food in there. It keeps its favorite rock in there as well. When it finds a clam, it floats on its back, sets the rock on its chest, and bangs the clam on the rock until it opens.

blocks.prompt: The Otter With a Pocket and a Rock
blocks.text: Most animals that live in cold seas stay warm with blubber. Blubber is a thick layer of fat under the skin. Seals have it. Whales have it. The sea otter has none. Instead it has fur, and its fur is the thickest of any animal on Earth. On one square inch of otter skin there can be about a million hairs. You have around a hundred thousand hairs on your whole head. All those otter hairs trap a layer of air, and that air keeps the cold water from ever touching the skin. This is why you often see a sea otter rolling and rubbing itself. It is not being silly. It is pushing fresh air back into its coat. A dirty coat lets water in, and an otter with wet skin gets dangerously cold. Staying warm this way burns a lot of energy, so a sea otter eats about a quarter of its own weight every day. Much of that food comes sealed inside a shell, so the otter uses a tool. It floats on its back, sets a rock on its chest, and hammers the shell down against it until the shell cracks. It carries that rock in a loose pocket of skin under its arm, and it often keeps the same one for years.

blocks.prompt: The Otter, the Urchin, and the Forest
blocks.text: Off the Pacific coast of North America there are forests underwater. They are made of kelp, a giant brown seaweed that grows up from the rocky bottom toward the light, sometimes a hundred feet tall. A kelp forest shelters fish, crabs, and seals the way a forest on land shelters birds. Kelp has an enemy. The sea urchin is a spiny ball that grazes along the bottom, chewing through the base of a kelp plant until the whole thing drifts away. When there are too many urchins, they can strip a forest down to bare rock. Scientists call that leftover wasteland an urchin barren. The sea otter is what stands between the two. An otter has no blubber, only fur, so it must eat about a quarter of its body weight every day just to stay warm. Urchins are an easy meal. A single otter can eat thousands of them in a year, and the urchins that survive stay wedged in cracks instead of grazing in the open. In the 1970s, biologists compared islands in Alaska where otters still lived with islands where fur hunters had wiped them out long ago. The difference was startling. The otter islands had thick kelp forests. The otterless islands had bare rock. Remove one animal and an entire forest disappears. Biologists call an animal with that much influence a keystone species, after the wedge at the top of a stone arch. Pull that one stone out and the arch does not sag. It falls.

blocks.prompt: The Fur That Almost Finished Them
blocks.text: In 1741 a Russian expedition led by Vitus Bering wrecked on a cold island in the North Pacific. The survivors ate sea otters to stay alive, then sailed home wearing their skins. That fur turned out to be the most valuable in the world. A single pelt could sell in the markets of China for more than a sailor earned in a year, and within a few decades ships from Russia, Britain, Spain, and America were working the coast from Japan to Baja California. The reason the fur was worth so much is the same reason the otter cannot live without it. A sea otter has no blubber. Every other marine mammal in cold water, the seals and the whales, carries a thick layer of fat beneath the skin. The otter carries air instead, held inside the densest coat on Earth: roughly a million hairs in a single square inch, about ten times what grows on your entire head. The air trapped in that coat is the only thing between the otter and water cold enough to kill it, which is why an otter spends hours a day grooming. A dirty patch of fur is a hole in its only jacket. The hunt ran for one hundred and seventy years. Perhaps three hundred thousand sea otters lived along the Pacific rim when Bering's crew came home. By 1911 fewer than two thousand remained, scattered in thirteen small colonies, and hunters could no longer find enough of them to make a voyage pay. That year four nations signed a treaty and the killing stopped. The otters were saved by their own scarcity almost as much as by the law. What happened next surprised everyone. As the otters returned, kelp forests returned with them. Otters eat sea urchins, urchins eat kelp, and coasts without otters had been ground down to bare rock. Watching that recovery is how biologists learned to call the otter a keystone species, one animal holding a whole system in place. Today about one hundred and twenty five thousand sea otters live in the North Pacific. In California, where every living otter descends from roughly fifty animals that survived along the cliffs of Big Sur, the count has stalled near three thousand.

notes: Enhydra lutris: heaviest weasel, smallest marine mammal
Water pulls heat from a body about 25x faster than air
Metabolism runs roughly 3x a land mammal its size

Keystone species, named in the Aleutians in the 1970s

blocks.prompt: A Coat, a Rock, and a Forest
blocks.text: Start with a problem in physics. Water pulls heat out of a body roughly twenty five times faster than air does. Any warm-blooded animal living in the North Pacific is therefore in a slow argument with the ocean, and almost every one of them settles it the same way: blubber. Seals, sea lions, whales, and walruses all carry a thick insulating layer of fat beneath the skin. The sea otter, alone among them, carries none. Its solution is a coat. Sea otter fur is the densest on Earth, packing something close to a million hairs into a single square inch, about ten times the number growing on a human head. The hairs are not the insulation, though. The air trapped between them is. A well-groomed otter wears a silver skin of bubbles underwater, and that layer, not fat, is what holds the cold at a distance. The arrangement is brilliant and it is fragile. Air leaks out. Dirt and oil let water reach the skin. So the otter grooms, obsessively, for hours every day, blowing and rubbing air back into its fur the way you would keep re-inflating a mattress with a slow leak. Insulation this thin has a running cost. A sea otter's metabolism burns about three times faster than that of a land mammal its size, and to feed that furnace it eats roughly a quarter of its own body weight daily: urchins, crabs, clams, abalone, mussels. Much of that food arrives sealed. So the otter does something almost no animal outside the primates does. It uses a tool. Floating on its back, it balances a stone on its chest and swings a shell down against it, again and again, until the shell gives. Otters keep favored stones, tucking them into a loose pouch of skin under the foreleg along with the day's catch, and individual otters develop their own habits with them. For a long time this was simply a charming set of facts about a charming animal. Then, in the 1970s, biologists working in the Aleutian Islands noticed something that changed how ecology is taught. Some islands had sea otters and dense underwater kelp forests. Neighboring islands, where fur hunters had eliminated otters two centuries earlier, had neither. They had bare rock crawling with sea urchins. The chain was short and brutal: otters eat urchins, urchins eat kelp, and kelp shelters nearly everything else. Take out the otter and the forest is grazed to nothing. The researchers called the otter a keystone species, borrowing the name of the wedge-shaped stone that locks a stone arch together. Pull it and the arch does not sag. It falls. The hunters were not incidental to this story. In 1741 the survivors of Vitus Bering's shipwrecked expedition sailed home wearing otter skins, and the fur trade that followed ran for one hundred and seventy years across the whole Pacific rim. Something like three hundred thousand otters became perhaps two thousand, scattered in thirteen remnant colonies, before a treaty signed by four nations in 1911 finally stopped the hunt. Every sea otter alive today descends from those survivors. In California, the entire population traces back to about fifty animals that held on beneath the cliffs of Big Sur. Recovery has been real but uneven. Roughly one hundred and twenty five thousand sea otters now live in the North Pacific, while the California population has stalled near three thousand, hemmed in by white sharks that bite otters and then leave them. The kelp, meanwhile, has returned wherever the otters have, and a growing kelp forest draws carbon out of the water. An animal hunted nearly to nothing for its coat turns out to have been maintaining a forest the entire time, for free, and nobody noticed until it was gone.
